examples: I'm from Chicago, but I live in Austin now.
I'm not sure that's the right address.
Sorry, I'm going to be about ten minutes late.
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: A contraction can never end a clause. Are you ready? — Yes, I am, never ✗ Yes, I'm. The same rule blocks ✗ I don't know where he's and ✗ Tell me what it's: with nothing after it, the verb has to be written out in full.

examples: You're the only one who noticed.

entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: you're vs your. If you can expand it to two words, it takes an apostrophe: You're late works as You are late, so it is you're; your flight cannot become you are flight, so it is your (твой, ваш). One sentence holds both: You're going to miss your flight. And yours never takes an apostrophe at all.

entries.type: be — the pronoun he + is (or + the auxiliary has)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: The 's is is or has, and the word after it decides. Before a noun, an adjective or an -ing form it is is: He's tired, He's working. Before a past participle it is has: He's gone, He's finished. Plain has meaning possession does not contract — He has a car, never ✗ He's a car, which would be read as he is a car. Possession does contract in has got: He's got a car.

entries.русский: это есть, оно уже (сокращение от it is или it has)
entries.type: be — the pronoun it + is (or + the auxiliary has)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: The 's is is or has: It's cold is is, It's been cold is has. It is never a possessive.
entries.contrast: it's vs its — the most-corrected pair in English. If you can expand it to two words, it takes an apostrophe: It's cold works as It is cold, so it's; the dog wagged its tail cannot become it is tail, so its (его, её). Possessives made from pronouns never take an apostrophe — its, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs. And there is no word its'.

examples: We're the ones who called you.
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: we're vs were. We're is we are, the present; were with no apostrophe is the past of be: We were ready then, and we're ready now. Many Americans reduce we're until it sounds just like were, so in writing the apostrophe is what carries the tense.

examples: They're the ones who organized the whole thing.

entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.contrast: they're vs their vs there — all three sound the same in American English. If you can expand it to two words, it takes an apostrophe: They're late works as They are late. Their is the possessive (их): their house. There is the place word and the empty subject of there is: over there, There are two left. One sentence with all three: They're over there with their kids.

entries.русский: есть, имеется (сокращение от there is или there has)
entries.type: be — the empty subject there + is (or + the auxiliary has)
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in writing, with one catch: there's in front of a plural (There's two seats left, There's a lot of people here) is everyday spoken American English but is marked wrong in school and in edited prose, which want There are two seats left
entries.ambiguity: The 's is is or has. Before a noun it is is: There's a problem. Before a past participle it is has: There's been a problem.
entries.contrast: there's vs theirs. Theirs is the possessive pronoun (The blue car is theirs) and never takes an apostrophe. Note also that the there of there's is not the place word: it is the empty subject that lets a sentence introduce something new.

entries.meaning: The contraction of here is, used to hand something over or to announce what comes next. ---
examples: Here's your receipt — have a good one.
Here's what I think we should do.
Here's the thing: nobody told the client.
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: Unlike there's, that's and he's, this 's is only ever is. There has been a delay contracts to There's been a delay, but here has been is not English, so here's has a single expansion. In speech it is also used in front of a plural — Here's your keys — which writing corrects to Here are your keys.

entries.contrast: who's vs whose. If you can expand it to two words, it takes an apostrophe: Who's coming? works as Who is coming? Whose is the possessive (чей) and cannot be expanded — Whose keys are these? is not ✗ Who is keys are these? The two often land in one sentence: Who's the guy whose car is blocking mine?

entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: The 's is is or has. How's the new job? is is; How's it been? is has. How's is also the standard American greeting frame — How's it going? — where nobody expects a detailed answer.

entries.meaning: The contraction of let us, used to propose doing something together.
examples: Let's grab lunch before the meeting.
Let's not talk about work tonight.
Let's say it takes three hours — we'd still get there by six.
entries.type: fixed — the 's is us, not is: the one contraction built on an object pronoun
entries.register: standard — normal in speech and in all but the most formal writing
entries.ambiguity: The 's of let's is us, the object pronoun — the one contraction in English where it is neither is nor has. And let's has no everyday full form: written out, let us is either formal and old-fashioned (Let us pray) or a literal request for permission (Let us in, Let us know when you land), and neither of those contracts — ✗ Let's in, ✗ Let's know.
entries.question form: Let's go, shall we? — the tag on a let's sentence is shall we?, never don't we? or won't we? The negative is let's not: Let's not argue about it. The British don't let's sounds odd in American English.
entries.contrast: let's vs lets. Lets with no apostrophe is the ordinary third-person verb — She lets the dog out at seven, This ticket lets you in twice. Let's is always a proposal to do something together, so the apostrophe marks the missing us.
